why_go: January brings cool mornings (10-25°C) and clear skies—ideal for walking the Brahmaputra riverbanks and exploring temple gardens. Fewer crowds than October-November, though cultural events thin out.
why_not: January's lower tourist numbers mean fewer riverboat crowds on the Brahmaputra, though cultural events thin out considerably.

things_to_do: Assam State Museum for colonial-era architecture
why_go: February offers warming days (12-27°C) and zero humidity—perfect for lingering on temple grounds and photographing the river. Spring festivals are still sparse.
why_not: Warm but still cool enough for walking—skip the sweat, keep the comfort.

why_go: March marks the arrival of spring (15-30°C) and Holi festivities. Temple grounds come alive with colour, and the Brahmaputra remains calm for cruises.
April brings Rongali Bihu—the Assamese New Year and biggest festival of the year. Temperatures remain pleasant (20-32°C), and the festival energy fills streets and temples.
pack_list: light cotton wear for warm days

why_not: Pre-monsoon heat and humidity (22-34°C) make outdoor sightseeing uncomfortable; use as a transit hub instead.
Brahmaputra flooding makes transport unreliable and swamps key sites during peak mela season. Monsoon breaks temple visits and riverboat access.
The Brahmaputra floods during peak monsoon, closing roads and stranding visitors for days. Peak rainfall (24-32°C with heavy downpours) disrupts all activities.
Monsoon flooding makes roads and attractions inaccessible through August. High water levels persist across the region.
Waterlogged streets and swollen rivers still pose navigation challenges as the city dries out. Monsoon rains linger through early September.

why_go: October brings post-monsoon clarity (18-30°C), clear skies, and Durga Puja festivities. The city comes alive with temple visits and cultural celebrations.
November offers the year's best weather (14-28°C), clear skies, and low humidity. Temple grounds are pristine, river visibility is maximum, and crowds are manageable.
December brings cool weather (10-25°C) and festive energy. Temple grounds are active, though crowds peak during Christmas and New Year weeks.
why_not: Holiday crowds peak during December, limiting spontaneity at major sites.

why_go: January is peak Hoysala season (16-29°C, dry). The 240-panel narrative frieze on the outer walls captures year-best light and clarity—a critical window for photographing the 12th-century carvings.
February is the driest month (17-31°C). The 240-panel frieze photography is at its year-best, and the stone carvings are cleanest. The Belur-Halebidu axis offers optimal viewing conditions.
March is the last cool month (19-33°C) before April heat peaks. Coffee Blossom time at adjacent Chikmagalur overlaps. Hotel rates ease 20 percent from February.
why_not: The stone carvings demand early starts—midday heat makes lingering uncomfortable.

why_go: April heat peaks above 35°C but Coffee Blossom reaches peak at adjacent Chikmagalur. Temple walks compress to morning hours only.
why_not: April heat peaks above 40°C, making temple exploration physically taxing.

why_go: May brings pre-monsoon thunderstorms and heat (23-35°C). Temple visits compress to early morning, then seek shade.
why_not: Peak heat and humidity make temple exploration uncomfortable in May.

why_go: June brings SW monsoon (22-30°C, 150-200mm rain). The interior of Hoysaleshwara Temple holds dry, and surrounding green-ghats opens for exploration. Crowds thin significantly.
why_not: Monsoon rains obscure the intricate stone carvings that make these 12th-century temples worth visiting.

things_to_do: temple interiors for shelter and meditation
why_go: July brings monsoon peak (21-28°C, 250-320mm rain) and full green-ghats landscape. The soapstone temple appears dark and dramatic against monsoon skies.
why_not: Monsoon mist softens the carved stone; go for solitude, not clarity.

why_go: August brings strong monsoon (21-28°C, 200-260mm rain) and lush green surroundings. The soapstone temple carvings take on dramatic moody light.
why_not: Monsoon rains create reflective surfaces on temple stone, but humidity accelerates moss growth on carved panels.

why_go: September brings monsoon ease (20-29°C, 150-200mm rain) and peak green-ghats backdrop. The Hoysala detail returns to view against verdant surroundings.
October opens the season (18-29°C, 80-120mm rain). Post-monsoon green-ghats provide dramatic backdrop, and the 240-panel frieze clarity builds toward peak.
November is peak season (17-28°C, dry). The 240-panel frieze reaches photography year-best detail and clarity. Karnataka Rajyotsava on Nov 1 marks the state foundation.
December is peak season (15-27°C, dry). The 240-panel frieze is at its year-cleanest. Christmas-NYE rates show moderate spike, but heritage experience is optimal.
January is peak Vijayanagara season (16-30°C, dry). Virupaksha and Vittala temples are at their year-cleanest light—optimal for monument photography and study.
February is the driest stretch (18-33°C). Boulder photography is at its year-best. The surreal landscape shows maximum clarity. Hotels remain at peak rate.
March is the last cool month (20-36°C). Daytime walks compress to morning hours. Hotel rates ease 25 percent, offering good value for optimal exploration windows.

why_not: April heat makes exploring sun-exposed ruins physically punishing without relief. Temperatures exceed 40°C and boulder radiation peaks.
Extreme heat makes exploring the exposed ruins physically dangerous in May. Granite re-radiates noon warmth to 50°C+ on exposed surfaces.

why_go: June brings SW monsoon light here (24-37°C, 60-90mm rain). Heat eases but trip still compressed to morning hours. Better to push visit to October.
why_not: Monsoon floods make ancient ruins inaccessible and pathways treacherous.

why_go: July brings SW monsoon (23-33°C, 90-120mm rain) and Tungabhadra in full flow. Walks viable AM/PM but water level makes riverside access unpredictable.
why_not: Monsoon flooding blocks the riverside hippie enclave you'd actually want to visit.

why_go: August brings monsoon tail (22-31°C, 80-110mm rain). River at full flow. Green carpet emerging. Solitude increases.
why_not: Monsoon rains make stone ruins treacherous and visibility poor for monument exploration.

why_go: September brings monsoon retreat (21-30°C, 50-80mm rain). Green carpet peaks. Last off-peak window before October season.
why_not: Monsoon rains make temple ruins slippery and trails harder to navigate safely.

why_go: October opens the season (19-31°C, 30-50mm rain). Green-carpet boulder field is spectacular. Heritage walks return mid-month to optimal conditions.
November brings Hampi Utsav (Nov 3-5) and Karnataka Rajyotsava (Nov 1). Weather is at year-best comfort (17-29°C, dry). Heritage walks reach peak optimal conditions.
December is peak season (15-28°C, dry). Christmas-NYE backpacker surge across the river. Heritage walks are at year-best comfort with optimal light.

why_not: At 3565m in January, deep snow makes this a technical winter trek requiring ice axes and crampons. Sankri base accessible but trek impossible.
Deep snow makes upper camps inaccessible without mountaineering experience and gear. Coldest month (-12 to 4°C) with route deep snow.

things_to_do: late-month trek attempts with snow gear
why_go: March trek season opens last week (-8 to 10°C). Snow patches still block higher sections, making the trek unpredictable. Experience required.
why_not: Snow patches still block the trail at 3565m, making the hard trek unpredictable in early March.

things_to_do: 4-5 day Har Ki Doon trek from Sankri
why_go: April opens trek season properly (-2 to 18°C). Rhododendron blooms splash colour across the trail. Snow is manageable. This is the cleanest spring window for a U-shaped valley trek.
May is peak spring (5-22°C). Wildflowers cover the meadow. Long daylight, clear skies. School-holiday trekking rush peaks. Highest visitor numbers.
June is pre-monsoon peak (8-25°C). Last clean window before monsoon closes operator departures. Clear skies and warm days make this ideal.

why_not: Monsoon rains trigger landslides on the access road and make trails treacherous with leeches. 200-300mm rainfall makes trekking dangerous.
Monsoon rains obscure mountain views and make steep trails treacherous. 250-350mm rainfall is peak worst conditions of the year.

why_go: September reopens trek season (100-150mm rain easing). Cleanest post-monsoon clarity arrives mid-month. Mountain views return. Low tourist crowds.
October is year-best month (4-20°C, dry, autumn colour peak). Glacier views are at maximum clarity. Operators run at peak capacity. This is the ideal window.
pack_list: camera with telephoto lens for glacier shots

why_go: November is late season (-2 to 14°C). First snow appears mid-month on upper sections. Trek season closes mid-late month. Operators still active.
why_not: Early snow makes trails treacherous and camps uninhabitable for most trekkers.
Snow accumulation makes the 3,565m pass nearly impassable in December without mountaineering experience. Sankri reachable but trek closed.

why_go: January is peak diving season (24-29°C, 30m visibility). Ferries are reliable. This is the premier window for underwater exploration. Book stays 30 days ahead.
February is the driest month (25-30°C, 30m+ visibility). Quieter than January after school holidays end mid-month. Premium conditions persist.
March is late peak (26-32°C, 25-28m visibility). Ferry schedules hold firm. Hotel rates are 25 percent below January, offering good value.
April is warm (28-33°C, 22-25m visibility). Ferries operate on schedule. Hotel rates are 35 percent off January. Off-peak with full operations.
May is the last clean month (28-33°C, 18-22m visibility dropping). Ferries hold schedule first 3 weeks. Visibility degradation begins as plankton blooms approach.
why_not: Plankton blooms reduce underwater visibility to 5-10 meters, making diving and snorkeling less rewarding.
Monsoon seas make ferry access unpredictable and diving completely off-limits. 450mm rain and frequent cancellations make trip unreliable.
Peak monsoon. 500mm rain. Dive operators closed. Ferries cancel routinely. Completely inaccessible.
Monsoon continues. 420mm rain, dive shops still closed, ferries unreliable. Island remains inaccessible.

why_go: September brings late monsoon (280mm rain). Dive shops reopen last week. Ferries patchy with 12-15m visibility. Infrastructure ramping up.
why_not: Ferry schedules remain chaotic as monsoon winds linger into early autumn.

why_go: October opens the season (130mm rain mostly first week). Visibility recovers to 20-25m. Hotel rates are 35 percent below December.
why_not: Water sports infrastructure still ramping up after monsoon closures.

why_go: November is strong shoulder (60mm rain, 24-30°C, 25m visibility). Diwali week books out, but otherwise excellent value. Calm seas return.
December is peak (23-29°C, 28-30m visibility). Christmas-NY commands 50 percent premium. Radhanagar conditions at year-best. Book resorts 45 days ahead.

why_not: Shrine closes seasonally and 15ft snow blocks all access routes. -25°C nights at Hemkund. Ghangaria buried.
Snow blocks road access and high altitude makes February too harsh for safe trekking. -28°C nights. Pre-yatra snow clearance not yet started.
Snow blocks the trail until late May, making March access impossible. Snow clearance starting but yatra still 8-10 weeks from open.
Snow blocks the approach roads until late May, making April access impossible. Yatra opens late May. Helicopter bookings open Apr 15.

why_go: May brings yatra opening (May 25, 2026) at -2 to 12°C at shrine. Helicopter operates from helibase. First-week pilgrim surge. Valley of Flowers opens as sister-trek.
why_not: Gurdwara won't open until late May; snow blocks the trail before then.

why_go: June is peak pilgrimage (0-15°C at shrine, dry). Steady pilgrim flow. Valley of Flowers opens for combined visit. This is the ideal pilgrimage window.
July brings monsoon (4-18°C). Heavy rain risk. Helicopter weather cancellations reach 30-40 percent. Valley of Flowers reaches full bloom. Trek-based pilgrimage works.
August brings monsoon (4-18°C) and Independence Day pilgrim surge. Valley of Flowers reaches tail. Trek-based access is primary; helicopter unreliable.
September brings monsoon retreat (2-15°C at shrine, dry late month). Cleanest post-monsoon clarity. Helicopter becomes reliable. Visibility peaks.
October brings yatra close (Oct 10, 2026) at -5 to 12°C. Final 10 days offer autumn colour. Cold but clear. Last window of the year.
why_not: Shrine closes by early October, and snow blocks the 4633m pass within weeks.
Snow blocks the mountain pass and shrine facilities shut down completely. Kapaat closed since Oct 10. Ghangaria empty.
Pilgrimage site completely snow-locked and inaccessible in winter months. -22°C nights at shrine.

who_should_go: coracle ride enthusiasts with low-flow tolerance
why_go: January is dry-season tail (18-30°C). Cauvery flow at 30 percent. Coracle rides workable but underwhelming compared to peak monsoon.
why_not: Water levels drop significantly in January, reducing the falls to a trickle.
Water flow drops significantly in February, reducing the falls to a trickle. 20 percent Cauvery flow and no multi-channel cascade.
Water levels drop significantly by March, reducing the falls to a trickle. 15 percent Cauvery flow. Falls essentially dry.
Water levels drop significantly in April, reducing the falls to a trickle. 25-37°C heat plus dry season.
Water levels drop severely in May, reducing the falls to a trickle. 26-38°C heat with dry conditions.

why_go: June brings SW monsoon upstream (24-32°C). Cauvery starts climbing. Falls still thin. Coracle rides unpredictable in spate.
why_not: Coracle rides—the main draw—are unpredictable in monsoon spate, so plan for hiking instead.

why_go: July brings Cauvery flood (24-30°C). Falls return to full multi-channel cascade by mid-month. This is the defining waterfall window.
August brings peak flow (23-30°C). Aadi-Perukku (Aug 3) celebrates Cauvery here. Lock beds early. Falls are at their year-most powerful.
September brings peak flow continuing (23-30°C). Karnataka SW retreat keeps flow at full. Hotels at peak. Fourth peak month of the season.
October brings NE monsoon (22-29°C). Cauvery flow holds at peak. Fourth peak month. This is the continuation of peak monsoon conditions.
November brings Karthigai pilgrim flow (20-28°C). Cauvery holds at 75 percent. Fifth peak month. Hotels at capacity with devotional energy.
pack_list: comfortable walking shoes for pilgrimage crowds

why_go: December brings flow descent (19-27°C, 60 percent). NE wraps mid-Dec. Falls at 60 percent. Christmas-NYE modest rates.
why_not: Water flow drops significantly post-monsoon, reducing the falls' visual impact.

why_go: January is peak Cardamom Hills season (14-28°C across district). Idukki Arch Dam permit at full tempo. Wildlife Sanctuary open. Dry conditions.
February is the driest month (16-30°C district-wide). KSEB dam permit at full hours. Wildlife Sanctuary at year-best visibility.
pack_list: camera with zoom lens for wildlife

why_go: March is the last cool window (18-32°C). KSEB permit available. Cardamom flowering visible at higher elevations. Trekking conditions optimal.
April brings pre-monsoon (20-34°C lower district). KSEB permit available. Cardamom flowering peaks. Heat tight outside hills.
why_not: Pre-monsoon humidity and occasional downpours make hiking less reliable than other seasons.

why_go: May is pre-monsoon peak (22-35°C lower district). First fortnight workable. Last 10 days bring SW-monsoon advance squalls. Humidity peaks.
why_not: Pre-monsoon haze dulls the cardamom hill views that make Idukki worth the climb.
Monsoon rains make most trails impassable and views obscured. NH85 landslide-prone. WLS suspends. 600-800mm rainfall.
Monsoon rains peak in July, making hill roads slippery and landslides common at this elevation. NH85 unreliable. WLS closed.
Monsoon rains peak in August, making hill treks slippery and landslide-prone. NH85 unreliable. WLS closed. Onam closes town.

why_go: September brings monsoon withdrawal (20-28°C, 400-500mm rain easing). WLS reopens late month. Cardamom harvest begins. Roads stabilizing.
October opens season (18-29°C, 200-300mm rain). NH85 stable. WLS open. Cardamom harvest peaks. Hotel rates 30 percent below December.
November builds high season (16-27°C district-wide). Cardamom harvest tail. Dam permit and WLS at full tempo. Rates climb 25 percent.
December is peak season (14-28°C district-wide). Christmas-NY rates 2-2.5x. Dam permits tight. NH85 packed. WLS at full capacity.
January is cool (4-22°C) and dry. Ima Keithel bustles. Temple grounds manageable. Pleasant for walking, though mornings require layers.
why_not: Morning cold requires layers, but afternoons warm pleasantly for exploring.

why_go: February brings warming (5-24°C) and Yaoshang festival celebrations. Temple grounds come alive. Spring energy builds.
why_not: Yaoshang festival crowds peak mid-February, so book accommodation well ahead.

why_go: March brings warmth (10-28°C) and Cheiraoba (Manipuri New Year, March/April). Spring energy. Temple grounds active. Culture peaks.
April is warm (14-30°C) but still pleasant. Pre-monsoon. Loktak Lake accessible before monsoon swells.
why_not: Pre-monsoon heat peaks toward month-end, making midday exploration uncomfortable.
Pre-monsoon humidity peaks before the rains arrive in June. 18-32°C with heavy moisture.
Monsoon flooding makes road access to Loktak Lake unsafe and unpredictable. 20-28°C with heavy rain.
Roads become impassable during peak monsoon rains, halting most transport in and out of the city.
August monsoon brings near-daily downpours that flood streets and disrupt travel plans.
Lingering monsoon humidity still makes outdoor sightseeing uncomfortable despite decreasing rainfall.

why_go: October brings post-monsoon clarity (14-28°C). Clear. Green. Pleasant. Loktak Lake accessible. Ima Keithel reopens fully.
November is the best month (10-26°C) with Sangai Festival—one of India's premier culture celebrations. Clear weather. Manipuri traditions showcase. Peak energy.
December brings cool weather (5-24°C) and dry conditions. Post-Sangai calm. Clear skies. Loktak Lake serene. Perfect exploration conditions.
